strengths: Significance: Representing pixels as averages of deformed template functions provides a useful framework for studying resolution and invariance. Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 identify conditions under which one labeled example per class suffices, offering an informative theoretical benchmark.

Originality: The valuable contribution is the statistical analysis connecting deformation coverings, resolution-dependent separation, and CNN complexity. The explicit filter construction in Theorem 4.2 gives an interpretable account of how convolution and global max-pooling can discriminate deformed templates.

Soundness and presentation: The alignment upper bounds have a coherent discretization-and-normalization argument, supported by extensive appendix derivations. The manuscript clearly distinguishes the three classifiers and illustrates their mechanisms.

Limitations and ethics: Sections 3.2 and 7 acknowledge background noise, occlusion, multiple objects, and sharp edges; Section 4.2 discusses the ideal-optimization assumption. These are appropriate disclosures. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the reported experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness: The CNN results require a support property that their stated assumptions do not guarantee. Assumption 2(i), requiring the template rectangle to lie inside A([0,1]^2), does not imply supp(f composed with A) lies inside [0,1]^2 for non-injective maps: additional preimages can occur outside the image. Nevertheless, Proposition B.4 and Equation (101) explicitly use this implication, and Equation (90) uses an injective change-of-variables equality. This matters because Section 4 expressly permits non-invertible deformations. An explicit support condition and corrected argument, or a restriction to invertible maps, are needed to justify the claimed generality.

Soundness and optimality: Theorem 3.8 lower-bounds ordinary normalized L2 distance, whereas the upper bounds use distances minimized over deformations in Equations (12) and (23). Appendix A.2 does not lower-bound those minimized distances, so it does not establish the advertised matching separation lower bound. The theorem also quantifies fixed templates before 'any d', although its construction makes f1 depend on d. Separately, the generic VC lower bound cited after Theorem 4.4 does not establish minimax optimality within this restricted deformation model.

Empirical evidence and significance: Section 5 generates training and test images by deforming selected templates. These experiments are useful illustrations, but do not test the central dependence on resolution, template separation, or deformation complexity. Figures 9 and 11 report only medians over ten repetitions with test sizes of 50 and 200, respectively, without uncertainty estimates or demonstrated robustness across template choices. Decreasing errors therefore provide limited validation of the quantitative theoretical claims.

Reproducibility: The manuscript provides no code link and omits deformation distributions/ranges, template identifiers, background-removal procedures, training epochs, batch sizes, and seeds. Table 1 specifies filter size, filter count, and fully connected width, but not the complete architecture or whether the experiments implement the theoretical weight constraints, pooling, and probability clipping. These omissions prevent reliable reproduction and assessment of the theory–experiment connection.

Presentation and originality: Pages 19–20 incorrectly characterize prior generalization bounds, including the uniform margin bounds in reference [8], as applying only to predictors independent of the data. Uniform bounds can apply to learned predictors. The defensible distinction is the explicit approximation analysis under the proposed image model; the current discussion overstates the departure from existing learning theory.
